subject: English
description: Common spelling traps, US vs UK, double letters, silent letters, 'ie/ei' rule

questions.explanation: Accommodate — one of the most commonly misspelled English words. Mnemonic: 'accommodate' has two c's, two m's, and an o between (think of 'two cottages and two motels need to accommodate guests'). Means: provide lodging or fit comfortably; adapt to. Other notorious double-letter words: occurrence (two c, two r), parallel (two l), embarrass (two r, two s), millennium (two l, two n), questionnaire (two n).
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Which spelling is CORRECT for the verb meaning 'to get / be given'?

options.option_text: Receive (i before e EXCEPT after c)

questions.explanation: Spelling rule: 'i before e, except after c' (when the sound is 'ee'). Examples: BELIEVE, ACHIEVE, RELIEVE, GRIEF (i before e); but RECEIVE, DECEIVE, CEILING, PERCEIVE, RECEIPT (e before i, after c). Exceptions to the exception: 'weird', 'seize', 'either', 'neither' (e before i, no c), and 'science', 'efficient' (i before e, after c — but these aren't the 'ee' sound). The rule strictly applies to long 'ee' sounds.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: The noun form of the verb 'maintain' is correctly spelled as:
questions.explanation: Maintenance — the noun from 'maintain'. Common error: people add an 'i' from the verb form, but the noun loses it. Pattern (verb → noun): maintain → maintenance, sustain → sustenance (no 'i' or 'a'), pertain → pertinence, attain → attainment (one of the few that keeps the 'a'). Other tricky -ance vs -ence words: existence (e), persistence (e), occurrence (e), independence (e), but acceptance (a), attendance (a), guidance (a). No simple rule — memorise.

questions.stem: Pick the correct spelling of the noun meaning 'a special right or advantage':
questions.explanation: Privilege — from Latin privi-legium = private law. No 'd' (a common error blends 'privilege' with 'edge'). Two i's, ends -lege. Other commonly misspelled: separate (NOT seperate; mnemonic: 'a rat in separate'); definitely (NOT definately); occasion (one s, two c — no, wait: ONE c, TWO s? actually one c, two c? — occasion has two c's no — let me recheck: o-c-c-a-s-i-o-n, two c's, one s — yes); calendar (NOT calender — calendar = the date one; calender = a roller machine).
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Which of these is the BRITISH-English spelling (vs American)?
questions.explanation: BRITISH vs AMERICAN spelling rules: (1) -our vs -or — colour/color, favour/favor, behaviour/behavior; (2) -re vs -er — centre/center, theatre/theater, metre/meter (BUT 'meter' for the device, both); (3) -ise vs -ize — organise/organize, realise/realize (Oxford English actually uses -ize too); (4) doubled L when adding suffix — travelling/traveling, modelling/modeling, cancelled/canceled; (5) -ce vs -se nouns — defence/defense, licence (n) license (v) in UK / 'license' for both in US; (6) judgement/judgment, programme/program (program for computers in UK too). Indian English follows BRITISH conventions.

questions.stem: The verb meaning 'to make someone feel awkward or self-conscious' is spelled:
questions.explanation: Embarrass — TWO r's, TWO s's. Means: cause to feel awkward / shy / ashamed. Memory aid: 'I had to face two Rs and two Ss when I was embarrassed'. Other 'two-pair' words: harass (one r, two s — UK; or harass two r? Actually it's harass: h-a-r-a-s-s — one r, two s in standard spelling, but 'harassed' is often misspelled as 'harrassed' or 'harased'); possess (one s pair, then two more s — p-o-s-s-e-s-s — two s, then two s = four s? Let me re-check: p-o-s-s-e-s-s = 4 letters s; mnemonic: 'I will possess the success'). Spelling errors most often involve missing one of a doubled-letter pair.

questions.stem: Identify the MISSPELLED word among the following four:
questions.explanation: Definitely — derived from 'finite' → de + FINIT + ely. NOT 'definately' (a high-frequency error in writing). Other classic traps: (1) Conscience — sci in the middle ('con-SCI-ence'). (2) Liaison — l-i-a-i-s-o-n — two i's, French origin. (3) Mischievous — only THREE syllables (mis-CHIE-vous), often mispronounced as 'mis-CHIE-vi-ous' (4 syllables) and mis-spelled as 'mischievious'. (4) Pronunciation — pro-nun-CI-A-tion (NOT 'pronounciation'). (5) Restaurant — restau-RANT (with -au-, French loanword).
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: The adverb meaning 'completely or entirely', derived from the adjective 'whole', is spelled as:

options.option_text: wholly — the standard, correct adverb form
wholely — common misspelling, the 'e' is dropped
holey — a real word meaning 'full of holes'

questions.explanation: 'Wholly' is correct — when an adjective ends in '-le', the 'e' is dropped before adding '-ly', giving 'wholly'. 'Wholely' is the most tempting wrong answer because learners instinctively add '-ly' directly to 'whole', but the spelling rule requires dropping the terminal 'e'.

questions.stem: The standard formal/academic plural of the noun 'phenomenon' is spelled as:

options.option_text: phenomenons — informal variant, not standard academic
phenomena — the correct Latin-derived plural form
phenomenas — an incorrect hybrid plural formation
phenomene — a completely invented incorrect form

questions.explanation: 'Phenomena' is correct — borrowed from Greek/Latin, 'phenomenon' forms its plural as 'phenomena', parallel to 'criterion/criteria'. 'Phenomenons' is heard colloquially but rejected in formal/academic writing. 'Phenomenas' wrongly treats 'phenomena' as if it were singular and re-adds '-s'.

questions.stem: The noun derived from the verb 'pronounce', meaning 'the way in which a word is spoken', is correctly spelled as:

options.option_text: pronounciation — keeps the 'pronounce' root but wrong
pronunciation — the correct standard dictionary form

questions.explanation: 'Pronunciation' is correct — despite the verb being 'pronounce', the noun drops the second 'o', giving 'pronun-' not 'pronoun-'. 'Pronounciation' is the most seductive error: test-takers preserve the verb root, but English nominalisation changes the vowel here. SSC and bank exams exploit this instinct regularly.

questions.stem: The verb meaning 'to take the place of something previously in use or authority' is correctly spelled as:

options.option_text: supercede — wrongly follows the '-cede' verb pattern
supersede — from Latin 'supersedere', to sit above
superseed — phonetic doubling, not etymologically sound
superceed — doubly wrong in both prefix and suffix

questions.explanation: 'Supersede' is correct — from Latin 'supersedere' (super + sedere, to sit), so the ending is '-sede', not '-cede'. 'Supercede' is the most tempting error because words like 'precede', 'recede', and 'concede' end in '-cede'; however, 'supersede' is the only common English word ending in '-sede'.

questions.stem: The noun used in formal writing to mean 'communication and cooperation between groups or organisations' is spelled as:

options.option_text: liason — omits the second 'i', a common misspelling
liaison — retaining both 'i' vowels from the French
liaision — inserts an extra syllable incorrectly
liasion — transposes the vowel sequence 'i-a' to 'a-i'

questions.explanation: 'Liaison' is correct — borrowed from French, it retains the unusual 'iai' vowel cluster. 'Liason' (omitting the second 'i') is the most common exam-level misspelling. 'Liasion' transposes the 'a' and second 'i'. Competitive exams favour this word because its French origin makes the vowel sequence non-intuitive for phonetic spellers.

questions.stem: The adjective used to describe an act showing gross disrespect or contempt for something considered sacred is spelled as:

options.option_text: sacreligious — wrongly derived from the word 'religion'
sacrilegious — correctly derived from the noun 'sacrilege'
sacriligious — a phonetic variant with no standard basis

questions.explanation: 'Sacrilegious' is correct — it derives from the noun 'sacrilege' (not from 'religion'), so the middle syllable is '-legi-' not '-reli-'. 'Sacreligious' is by far the most seductive error: candidates embed the word 'religious' inside it because the meaning relates to religion, but the Latin root is 'sacrilegus' (temple robber), making '-reli-' wrong.

questions.stem: The noun referring to a printed or digital set of questions used for survey research or data collection is spelled as:

options.option_text: questionaire — drops one 'n', the most frequent error
questionnairre — adds an extra 'r', an over-correction
questionairre — wrong in both the middle and end parts
questionnaire — retains the French double 'n' and '-aire'

questions.explanation: 'Questionnaire' is correct — borrowed from French, it keeps the double 'n' (question + naire) and the '-aire' suffix. 'Questionaire' (single 'n') is the most common misspelling and a favourite distractor in SSC and bank exams. 'Questionnairre' is an over-correction, doubling the 'r' by analogy with words like 'bizarre', which does not apply here.
